title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 118 (Minutes of proceedings of general meeting, meeting of Board of Directors and other meeting and resolutions passed by postal ballot)

content.overview: Section 118 requires covered meeting and postal-ballot minutes to be prepared, signed and kept within thirty days in consecutively numbered books, and requires compliance with notified Secretarial Standards. Duly kept minutes are evidence and create the statutory presumption described in subsection (8), subject to contrary proof. The section also prescribes company/officer penalties for default and imprisonment/fine for tampering.

content.study: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 118 (Minutes). Minutes of general meetings, class meetings, meetings of creditors, Board and Board committees, and resolutions passed by postal ballot must be prepared, signed and kept in the prescribed manner within thirty days in books with consecutively numbered pages. The section requires a fair and correct summary and compliance with applicable notified Secretarial Standards. Duly kept minutes are evidence of proceedings; until the contrary is proved, the meeting is deemed duly called and held, proceedings deemed to have taken place, postal-ballot resolutions deemed duly passed and specified appointments deemed valid. A report of proceedings may not be circulated or advertised at the company's expense unless it includes the matters required by the section. For non-compliance, the company is liable to a penalty of ₹25,000 and every officer in default to ₹5,000. A person found guilty of tampering with minutes is punishable with imprisonment up to two years and a fine of at least ₹25,000 and up to ₹1,00,000. The topic remains under source and current-law review.

sections.heading: Preparation and maintenance
sections.body: Minutes of covered general meetings, meetings of classes of shareholders or creditors, Board and committee meetings, and resolutions passed by postal ballot must be prepared, signed and kept in the prescribed manner within thirty days in minute-books with consecutively numbered pages.

sections.heading: Contents and Secretarial Standards
sections.body: Minutes must contain the matters required by section 118, including a fair and correct summary of proceedings and specified appointment details. Applicable Secretarial Standards specified by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India and approved by the Central Government must be observed.

sections.heading: Evidentiary effect and presumption
sections.body: Minutes kept in accordance with the section are evidence of the proceedings. Until the contrary is proved, the meeting is deemed duly called and held, proceedings are deemed to have duly taken place, postal-ballot resolutions are deemed duly passed and specified appointments are deemed valid.

sections.heading: Publication of meeting reports
sections.body: A document purporting to report proceedings of a general meeting may not be circulated or advertised at the company's expense unless it includes the matters required by section 118 to be contained in the minutes.

sections.heading: Default and tampering
sections.body: For default in complying with section 118, the company is liable to a penalty of ₹25,000 and every officer in default to ₹5,000. A person found guilty of tampering with minutes is punishable with imprisonment up to two years and a fine not less than ₹25,000 and up to ₹1,00,000.

examples.title: Timely minutes
examples.body: The company prepares, signs and enters covered meeting minutes within thirty days, maintains consecutively numbered minute-books and applies the relevant Secretarial Standards.

examples.title: Tampering with minutes
examples.body: Where a person is found guilty of tampering with meeting minutes, identify the separate criminal penalty provision in section 118(12) rather than treating the matter as a routine recordkeeping default.

hypotheticals.question: What is the evidentiary effect of minutes kept in accordance with section 118?
hypotheticals.analysis: They are evidence of the proceedings. Until the contrary is proved, subsection (8) provides the stated presumptions about due calling and holding of the meeting, proceedings, postal-ballot resolutions and specified appointments. This is not an irrebuttable presumption.

hypotheticals.question: A company fails to comply with section 118, and a person is found guilty of tampering with minutes. What penalty categories must be distinguished?
hypotheticals.analysis: Subsection (11) imposes a penalty of ₹25,000 on the company and ₹5,000 on every officer in default for non-compliance. Subsection (12) separately provides imprisonment up to two years and a fine between ₹25,000 and ₹1,00,000 for a person found guilty of tampering.

misconceptions.trap: Treating minutes as conclusive proof or as curing every defect in the underlying meeting.
misconceptions.correction: Minutes are evidence, and subsection (8)'s presumption applies until the contrary is proved; minutes do not independently cure every substantive defect.

misconceptions.trap: Treating every minute-book default and tampering as the same penalty event.
misconceptions.correction: Subsections (11) and (12) provide distinct consequences for non-compliance and tampering.

misconceptions.trap: Ignoring the thirty-day maintenance period or the consecutively numbered book requirement.
misconceptions.correction: Check the prescribed manner, time period and minute-book structure as separate compliance requirements.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What does section 118 require?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Minutes of specified meetings and postal-ballot resolutions must be prepared, signed and kept within thirty days. Applicable notified Secretarial Standards must be followed. Duly kept minutes are evidence of proceedings.

examTips: Mention Secretarial Standards and the thirty-day period.
revisionPoints: Covered minutes must be prepared, signed and kept within thirty days in consecutively numbered books.
Applicable Secretarial Standards must be observed.
Duly kept minutes are evidence and trigger subsection (8)'s rebuttable presumption.
Tampering: imprisonment up to two years and fine ₹25,000–₹1,00,000.
